Drummer Jimmie Nicol waits for the plane which will take him back to "real life" after sitting in for an ill Ringo Starr during Beatlemania. Melbourne, Australia. 1964

When Ringo Starr collapsed with tonsillitis and was hospitalized on the eve of The Beatles' 1964 Australasian tour, the band's manager Brian Epstein and producer George Martin urgently discussed the feasibility of using a stand-in drummer rather than cancelling part of the tour. Martin suggested Jimmie Nicol as he had drummed on a 'Top Six' budget label album of Beatles cover versions which meant that he already knew the songs.

Nicol played a total of eight shows until Starr rejoined the group in Melbourne, Australia. He was unable to say goodbye to The Beatles as they were still asleep when he left, and he did not want to disturb them. At the airport, manager Brian Epstein presented him with a cheque for £500 and a gold wrist watch inscribed: 'From The Beatles and Brian Epstein to Jimmy – with appreciation and gratitude.'

Martin later paid tribute to Nicol whilst acknowledging the problems he experienced in trying to re-adjust to a normal life again: 'Jimmie Nicol was a very good drummer who came along and learnt Ringo's parts very well. He did the job excellently, and faded into obscurity immediately afterwards.' Nicol himself expressed his disillusionment several years later: 'Standing in for Ringo was the worst thing that ever happened to me. Until then I was quite happy earning £30 or £40 a week.
